data.name: Place1Detail1
data.value: Huge, perfectly rounded boulders cover the shore of the Barents Sea. Waves have been polishing them for thousands of years, and the beach now looks as if a dragon left its clutch here. The stones are most dramatic in a storm, when the ocean rolls them with a deep rumble.

data.name: Place1Detail2
data.value: The beach lies beyond the village, on the way to Batareysky waterfall. Walk carefully: the stones get slippery in the rain. The best light for photos is the polar sunset, when the low sun paints the boulders in warm gold.

data.name: Place2Detail1
data.value: At low tide the ribs of early 20th-century wooden fishing ships rise out of the bay. Teriberka was once a major centre of coastal fishing, and the old schooners lived out their days right by the shore.

data.name: Place2Detail2
data.value: Today the blackened hulls are the most recognisable view of Teriberka — they appeared in “Leviathan” and dozens of documentaries. Come at low tide, when you can walk almost up to the ships.

data.name: Place3Detail1
data.value: Lake Maloye Batareyskoye spills over the edge of a rocky canyon and falls straight into the Barents Sea. It is one of the few places in the world where a waterfall meets the ocean.

data.name: Place3Detail2
data.value: The name comes from a WWII artillery battery that defended the entrance to the bay; its positions survive nearby. A trail across stony tundra leads to the waterfall — wear non-slip shoes.

data.name: Place4Detail1
data.value: From the clifftop viewpoints you look out at the open ocean: beyond the horizon, all the way to the Pole, there is only water and ice. In winter the sea does not freeze thanks to the warm Gulf Stream.

data.name: Place4Detail2
data.value: In spring and early summer you can spot whales and orcas from the shore, and kittiwakes nest on the cliffs. Bring a thermos: the wind at the edge of the continent almost never stops.

data.name: Place5Detail1
data.value: From September to April it is dark enough above the Arctic Circle to see the aurora. We track solar activity and cloud cover and take the group to spots free of light pollution — the odds of seeing the lights in one night of hunting are high.

data.name: Place5Detail2
data.value: The aurora is capricious: sometimes a faint green haze, sometimes the whole sky dancing in waves from horizon to horizon. Dress in layers — the hunt means several hours in the cold, with hot tea and a tripod.

data.name: Place6Detail1
data.value: The road to Teriberka runs through true Arctic tundra: hills, lakes, dwarf birches and carpets of reindeer moss. In summer the tundra blooms with cloudberries and fireweed; in winter it becomes an endless white desert.

data.name: Place6Detail2
data.value: Along the way we stop at panoramic points — from here the Kola Peninsula looks just like in films about the North. With luck, we will meet reindeer.

data.name: Place7Detail1
data.value: A mountain horseshoe east of the Khibiny hides Seydozero, the sacred lake of the Sami. From the cliff above the water stares Kuyva — a petrified giant, as the legend goes — surrounded by cirques, gorges and screes where some of the rarest minerals are found.

data.name: Place7Detail2
data.value: A one-day route: approach via the settlement of Revda, a hike over the pass and a descent to the lake. The trail is easy but rocky — trekking shoes required. White nights in summer; in September the tundra blazes gold and crimson.

data.name: Place8Detail1
data.value: Geologists' Pass is a saddle by Mount Alluaiv in the Lovozero Tundras, just over a kilometre above the sea. It offers one of the best panoramas of the Kola: Lake Umbozero spreads below, with the wall of the Khibiny rising beyond.

data.name: Place8Detail2
data.value: We go up in prepared off-road trucks — the road itself is an adventure. It is windy on top even in summer, so bring a warm jacket. In winter the pass drowns in snow, and on clear nights it is a great spot to hunt the aurora.

data.name: Place9Detail1
data.value: The southern shore of the Kola along the White Sea is old Pomor country. At Cape Korabl amethyst druses show right through the rocks, and near the village of Kuzomen lies the world's northernmost desert — kilometres of red sands roamed by wild horses.

data.name: Place9Detail2
data.value: Along the way: fishing stations, wooden churches and beaches where the sea walks away over the horizon at low tide. It is a long drive, so the Tersky Coast is a full-day tour with an early start and a sunset over the White Sea.

data.name: Place10Detail1
data.value: Umba is one of the oldest Pomor villages of the Kola Peninsula, more than five centuries old. Wooden houses stand over the rapids of the Umba river, and the museum of Pomor life keeps the stories of living off the sea for generations.

data.name: Place10Detail2
data.value: Nearby lies Lake Kanozero, whose islands hold thousands of rock carvings up to six thousand years old. In summer Umba is the capital of rafting and fishing — people come for salmon, cloudberries and silence.

data.name: Place11Title
data.value: Varzuga

data.name: Place11Text
data.value: A 15th-century village with a wooden church built without a single nail.

data.name: Place11Detail1
data.value: Varzuga stands on the river of the same name, fifteen kilometres from the sea — one of the oldest Russian settlements of the Kola Peninsula, first mentioned in 1466. Its wonder is the tented Dormition church of 1674: hewn from pine without a single nail, it still withstands the northern storms.

data.name: Place11Detail2
data.value: The Varzuga is one of Europe's finest salmon rivers: in season anglers come from all over the country. On the way — the Kuzomen sands, where feral horses roam the dunes.

data.name: Place12Title
data.value: Stone labyrinth

data.name: Place12Text
data.value: A four-thousand-year-old spiral of boulders on the White Sea shore.

data.name: Place12Detail1
data.value: Near Umba the shore keeps a stone labyrinth — a spiral of boulders laid out by the ancient people of the North some four thousand years ago. Such labyrinths dot the whole White Sea coast, and their purpose is still a mystery: a fish trap, a sanctuary or a map of hunting grounds.

data.name: Place12Detail2
data.value: We walk to the labyrinth along the shore: a short stroll with views over the bay and the guide's stories about the Pomors and the ancient cultures of the White Sea. The best view is from the hill — only from above does the spiral show itself whole.

data.name: Place13Title
data.value: Sredny and Rybachy

data.name: Place13Text
data.value: Land's end beyond Murmansk: the Musta-Tunturi ridge and the open-ocean shore.

data.name: Place13Detail1
data.value: Sredny and Rybachy are the northernmost peninsulas of European Russia. The track climbs over the Musta-Tunturi ridge and follows rocky shores past old wartime positions; the coast rewards you with waterfalls, seabird colonies and a horizon-wide view of the open Arctic Ocean.

data.name: Place13Detail2
data.value: The route is fully off-road and takes the whole day. Bring windproof layers and food: the peninsulas have no cafes and no mobile coverage — only tundra, ocean and wind.

data.name: FactLabel
data.value: Did you know?

data.name: Place1Detail3
data.value: Each boulder weighs tens or even hundreds of kilograms, yet in a strong storm the ocean rolls them like pebbles — by morning the beach can look different from the day before. In winter the stones wear a crust of ice and glitter in the low sun like glass.

data.name: Place1Fact
data.value: Taking the “eggs” away is forbidden: the shore is a protected natural area, and without its boulders the beach would simply vanish.

data.name: Place2Detail3
data.value: Most of the vessels are wooden fishing schooners and motorboats: when coastal fishing was wound down, the fleet was hauled onto the shallows and left there. The cold salty water preserved the timber, so the ribs of the hulls have stood for more than half a century.

data.name: Place2Fact
data.value: In the mid-20th century Teriberka was one of the main fishing villages of the Murman coast, with its own fish factory and ship-repair workshops.

data.name: Place3Detail3
data.value: The waterfall drops to the sea in several steps over dark rocks, and the canyon works like a horn — you hear the roar long before you arrive. In spring, during snowmelt, the flow is at its strongest; by late summer it calms down and turns crystal clear.

data.name: Place3Fact
data.value: Even in hard frosts the waterfall never freezes solid — under the ice you can hear the water still running.

data.name: Place4Detail3
data.value: Off Teriberka the warm Atlantic current meets Arctic waters, which makes the sea unusually alive: cod and wolffish, red king crab, and humpback whales that follow the capelin right up to the shore. This is where people come from all over the country for whale watching.

data.name: Place4Fact
data.value: The Barents Sea averages only about 220 metres deep — a shallow shelf by ocean standards, which is why it is so rich in fish.

data.name: Place5Detail3
data.value: The aurora is born 100–300 kilometres up: particles of the solar wind collide with the atmosphere, oxygen glows green and nitrogen adds violet flashes. The stronger the solar flare, the further south the lights reach — but over Teriberka they appear even on quiet nights.

data.name: Place5Fact
data.value: The best months for the hunt are September and March: geomagnetic storms are noticeably more frequent around the equinoxes.

data.name: Place6Detail3
data.value: The tundra only looks empty: hundreds of species of mosses and lichens live here, and reindeer lichen grows just a few millimetres a year. That is why we keep to the trails — the tundra takes decades to heal a wheel track or a campfire scar.

data.name: Place6Fact
data.value: A dwarf birch that barely reaches your ankle can be more than a hundred years old.

data.name: Place7Detail3
data.value: In the Sami legend Kuiva is a giant struck down by the lightning of the gods; his dark silhouette remained on the cliff above the water. Science explains the figure as a pattern of mosses and wet streaks, yet the lake keeps its special aura: for centuries the Sami held it sacred and would not even fish here without need.

data.name: Place7Fact
data.value: The figure of Kuiva on the cliff is 74 metres tall — higher than a twenty-storey building.

data.name: Place8Detail3
data.value: The Lovozero and neighbouring Khibiny tundras are ancient alkaline massifs and a treasury of rare minerals: here they find eudialyte, known as “Sami blood”, and dozens of stones hardly found anywhere else in the world.

data.name: Place8Fact
data.value: These mountains are hundreds of millions of years old — glaciers and wind have worn them down into gentle stone plateaus.

data.name: Place9Detail3
data.value: Amethysts at Cape Korabl were mined by the Pomors, and the trade was first set up by the monks of the Solovetsky Monastery — until the Ural deposits were discovered, the Tersky coast remained Russia's main source of jewellery amethyst. Today the cape is a geological monument: you may admire the druses, but not chip them off.

data.name: Place9Fact
data.value: The desert at Kuzomen is man-made: the sands spread after the forests were felled for salt works and the dunes were broken by grazing cattle.

data.name: Place10Detail3
data.value: The Kanozero petroglyphs were found by accident: on 5 July 1997 museum workers from Revda were rafting down the Umba and noticed carvings on an island rock. More than 1,200 images have been described since — elk, whales, boats, shamans; a protective dome now covers the main rock.

data.name: Place10Fact
data.value: Umba was first mentioned in written sources in 1466 — it is older than many of Russia's northern cities.

data.name: Place11Detail3
data.value: Varzuga was once the pearl capital of the North: river pearls were fished here to embroider Pomor dresses and icon frames. Today the village lives on salmon and pilgrims — people come to see how the Dormition church's timber has held for over three centuries without a single nail.

data.name: Place11Fact
data.value: The tent roof of the Dormition church rises 34 metres — all of it pine timberwork raised without nails in 1674.

data.name: Place12Detail3
data.value: Stone spiral “babylons” are scattered across the whole White Sea and Scandinavian north; the Kandalaksha one is among the most accessible, reached by a walking path along the bay. Walking inside the lanes is frowned upon — out of respect for its age, and so as not to shift stones that have lain for millennia.

data.name: Place12Fact
data.value: One hypothesis says the spiral “entangled” the soul of a caught fish so it could not return to the sea and lead the catch away.

data.name: Place13Detail3
data.value: The Musta-Tunturi ridge the road climbs over is the only place where the enemy failed to cross the USSR land border in the whole of the Second World War: the front line stood still here from the first day of the war until 1944. Shell casings still turn up among the rocks, and a museum of the peninsulas' defence works at the foot of the ridge.

data.name: Place13Fact
data.value: Cape Nemetsky on Rybachy is the northernmost point of European Russia.

data.name: ItineraryTitle
data.value: Your day in Teriberka

data.name: ItinerarySubtitle
data.value: A full day: we meet you at the airport or in town, drive you in comfort to the highlights of the coast and bring you back in the evening.

data.name: ItineraryNote
data.value: The order and availability of stops may change with the weather — the North always has the final say.

data.name: Itinerary1Title
data.value: Airport or city pickup

data.name: Itinerary1Text
data.value: We collect you at the airport or at an agreed point in Murmansk, Apatity or Kirovsk and travel in a comfortable minivan. From Murmansk, the road across the tundra takes about two hours.

data.name: Itinerary2Title
data.value: Old Teriberka

data.name: Itinerary2Text
data.value: Walk by the ship graveyard and learn how the settlement by the Barents Sea has changed.

data.name: Itinerary3Title
data.value: Ocean coast

data.name: Itinerary3Text
data.value: Visit Dragon Eggs beach and take in open views across the Barents Sea.

data.name: Itinerary4Title
data.value: Batareysky waterfall

data.name: Itinerary4Text
data.value: Walk across the tundra to the waterfall dropping from the cliffs towards the sea.

data.name: Itinerary5Title
data.value: Seafood lunch

data.name: Itinerary5Text
data.value: Fresh cod, scallops and fish soup — lunch in Teriberka before the drive back.

data.name: Itinerary6Title
data.value: Return to the city

data.name: Itinerary6Text
data.value: After a full day we drive back and drop you at the agreed point in Murmansk, Apatity or Kirovsk.

data.name: SeasonsTitle
data.value: Teriberka through the seasons

data.name: SeasonsSubtitle
data.value: Every season has its own North — we will help you choose yours.

data.name: Season1Title
data.value: November — April

data.name: Season1Text
data.value: Aurora season, snowy tundra and short daylight hours. Extra-warm clothing is essential.

data.name: Season2Title
data.value: May — August

data.name: Season2Text
data.value: Midnight sun, longer walks, open trails and vivid tundra colours.

data.name: Season3Title
data.value: September — October

data.name: Season3Text
data.value: Golden tundra, autumn storms and dark skies returning for aurora hunting.

data.name: SeasonNote
data.value: The northern lights, whales and good weather are natural phenomena and cannot be guaranteed.

data.name: PracticalTitle
data.value: Before you travel

data.name: PracticalSubtitle
data.value: Quick answers to the questions travellers ask most often before Teriberka.

data.name: Faq1Question
data.value: What if the road closes because of the weather?

data.name: Faq1Answer
data.value: Safety comes before the programme. We will contact you and offer a new date or another available route.

data.name: Faq2Question
data.value: What should I wear?

data.name: Faq2Answer
data.value: Coastal weather changes quickly. Bring a windproof outer layer, warm layers and shoes with non-slip soles.

data.name: Faq3Question
data.value: Can children join?

data.name: Faq3Answer
data.value: Yes, but the route takes a full day and includes walks over rocky terrain. Tell the operator your child's age.

data.name: Faq4Question
data.value: Do I pay when I submit the form?

data.name: Faq4Answer
data.value: No. We first confirm the date, programme and final price; then you decide whether to book.

data.name: Faq5Question
data.value: How long is the tour?

data.name: Faq5Answer
data.value: A full day: we leave Murmansk in the morning and return in the evening. We confirm exact times when you book — they depend on the season and daylight.

data.name: Faq6Question
data.value: What happens after I send a request?

data.name: Faq6Answer
data.value: We call you back on the number you gave, confirm the date, group size and wishes, and quote the final price. Booking happens only once you agree.

data.value: Name the route you want when we call — we will find a date for that one too
